text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Labour Department (AMS) figures on the employment situation forecast open unemployment falling to 7.1 percent next year from 8.0 percent in 1996. Taken together with the people who are without work and on retraining schemes, the jobless figure falls to 12.5 percent in 1997 from this year's 12.6 percent.

-The opposition Conservative, Liberal and Christian Democratic parties will vote on Friday against Prime Minister Goran Persson in a parliamentary no-confidence vote, but the premier looks certain to win after three other non-government parties said they would either abstain or support the ruling Social Democrats. The premier angered Swedish politicians by appearing to praise China's political stability during an official visit in Beijing this month.

-Conservative leader Carl Bildt, with his lofty pronouncements yesterday seeking an all-party compromise over Sweden's China policy, is the only winner from the decision by his and two other opposition parties to force the no-confidence vote. Bildt, temporarily absent from Swedish politics on an EU mission in Bosnia, emerges as a professional who would never have become involved in this amateurish political wrangling, the paper wrote.

-TV channels belonging to the Kinnevik group, Sports channel, TV6, ZTV and TV 1000 together show a loss of 500 million crowns, leading to 20 job losses out of a total 70 in ZTV. From January, ZTV, TV6 and the Sports channel will become pay-channels because advertising revenues do not cover costs. But Pelle Tornberg, managing director of Kinnevik's Modern Times Group, says this is not a crisis and the media group will continue to market aggressively.

-The Swedish government is negotiating with Finnair and Sabena on a deal for its officials to fly at reduced rate between Stockholm and Brussels, after Nordic European Airlines said it will stop its service between the two capitals from December 2, citing lack of support by Swedish civil servants. DAGENS INDUSTRI

-The Stockholm bourse says private meetings between companies and analysts, from which the public and press are excluded, break bourse rules on disclosure and must stop. Recently Pharmacia & Upjohn's share price fell 14 percent after such a meeting. Bourse officials will make their views known at a seminar for companies and brokers. Mats Wilhelmsson, head of the bourse's market supervision, said he was unhappy with what was regarded as "analyst massaging."

- Minister of Communications Ines Uusmann says the public does not want state-owned Telia, the country's largest telecommunications company, to be privatised. Management of the company say investment of between five and 10 billion crowns is needed immediately. Uusmann regards herself as an active shareholder on behalf of the state, with ambitions for Telia to play a lead role in the IT revolution.

-Astra AB's number one product Losec, an ulcer treatment, is being pirated in China. The company is estimated to lose more than 100 million crowns in potential sales this year from the counterfeit goods, according to Raymond Ho, managing director for Astra Wuxi with responsibility for China. Svenska Elekta and other companies have similarly complained that their products are illegally copied in China. -- Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1017
